title: Your map of suffering
hookLine: which teachings and practices actually help you?

cards: An old trail map, folded and refolded until the creases have gone soft. Someone has written on it in pencil. A circle around a spring: good water.
An X on a shortcut: don't, it floods. A star on a ledge: sat here, saw everything. The printed map shows the whole mountain.
The pencil shows what one walker learned on it. For weeks now this path has been walking through suffering, with teachings from many traditions. Today, the pencil comes out.

teach.b: First, a map, not a creed. A creed says what is true for everyone. A map of suffering says something smaller and more useful: what has actually helped this one person, on this one road.
It doesn't have to settle why suffering exists. It only has to mark the springs and the floods. Second, look back at the road so far.
The Buddha's teaching of the second arrow: the pain, and then the pain we add to it. The psalmist's question, how long, said straight to God. Patience, sabr, in the Qur'an.

The friends who sat with Job in silence, before they ruined it by talking. Viktor Frankl's last freedom, the choice of an attitude. These last two weeks: a small mercy, a quiet hour, one day at a time, a city rising.

teach.h: WHAT WE'VE WALKED, EACH IN ITS PLACE.
teach.b: Each came from its own tradition, and each stays with its own source. Your map can hold several without blending them into one teaching. Third, two columns.
On one side, what helps. On the other, what doesn't, even when it's supposed to. Some people find advice makes things worse, and silence helps.
Some find a practice that works on a bad day and fails on a terrible one. Both are worth writing down. An honest map has X marks too.
Fourth, maps change. A map drawn young looks different later on. A teaching that meant nothing last year may be the spring you need next year.
So the map stays in pencil.
Write it today, and expect to erase.

how: Some people keep a written list of what helps in hard times, from scripture verses and prayers to walks and phone numbers, and some therapists and chaplains help people draw up such a plan before a crisis.

o: the pain we add on top of pain, in the Buddha's image
a second injury that follows the first by chance
the spare arrow an archer keeps in case the first misses

games.q: which teaching came from where — tap the pairs.
p: the Buddha: the pain we add
Viktor Frankl: the choice of attitude

s: a map of suffering has to pick one tradition's answer
it can hold several, each kept with its own source, without blending them.
an honest map marks what doesn't help, too
two columns: the springs and the floods.
once drawn, the map is finished
it stays in pencil; what helps can change over the years.

games.q: a friend's advice, meant kindly, always makes your bad days worse. where does it go on the map?
o: leave it off; it was meant well.
games.why: an honest map has X marks too. writing it down isn't unkind; it's knowing the terrain.

practice: On paper or a phone note, draw a line down the middle: on the left, what helps when things are hard, a teaching, a practice, a person, a place, a song; on the right, what doesn't help, even if it's meant to.
Three on each side is plenty, so don't think too long, then look at the left column and notice which one you'd reach for first. If you pray, prayer may be on your map; it belongs there if it helps.

wordCard.voice: Second arrow, the Buddha's teaching that there's the pain, and then the pain we add to it, one entry on this map of suffering. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: what helps me. An honest map has X marks too. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

sources.ref: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning
